title: arrival-entropy-concurrency-matching-exploration
content:
TL;DR

This is an exploratory draft for a different way to reason about continuous-batching capacity: match instantaneous slot supply elasticity to an "arrival entropy" signal instead of fixed window sizes. The goal is to produce a small, auditable spreadsheet and a set of low-effort experiments to validate whether entropy-aware concurrency rules reduce p95 violations and unit cost for mixed short/long requests.

Context and motivation

- Problem: continuous batching heuristics we've used (fixed window, token-pack-based reservoir) struggle under multimodal arrival shapes (bursty + sustained) and mixed prompt lengths. Current spreadsheets show we either over-provision headroom (costly) or under-provision (p95 spikes).
- Hypothesis: an arrival-entropy metric (see below) that quantifies unpredictability in short windows can be used to scale slot supply elasticity (how many slots we temporarily allow beyond steady-state) and to tune the reservoir release policy. This gives better tail control for the same average utilization.

Definitions & high-level model overview

- slot: one execution concurrency unit (a GPU slot that can serve a continuous-batch).
- supply curve S(u): number of slots available as function of utilization u (0..1). We model S(u) as baseline + elastic term * f(entropy).
- arrival entropy H_t: Shannon-style measure over short inter-arrival time histogram at time t (discretized over 100ms bins). Higher H -> more spread out unpredictability; low H -> steady periodic arrivals.
- request size distribution P(L): empirical histogram of prompt+reply token counts (we keep separate short/medium/long buckets).
- p95 latency estimate: two-term model: deterministic service-time term (queueingless) + queueing tail term proportional to reservoir overflow probability.

Assumptions (for spreadsheet prototype)

1) Service time per token is approximated by a single constant per model variant (baseline kernel), with additive overhead for context-switch. Use 0.85ms/token for x1 model on A100s as placeholder (replace with profiler numbers).
2) In-flight batching effect: tokens from multiple requests pack into batch efficiency factor E(batch_size) which reduces per-token time by ~1/(1 + alpha * (batch_size-1)) — alpha calibrated from perf bench.
3) Short-term arrivals are stationary over 5s windows for entropy calculation; we recompute entropy every 250ms sliding window.
4) Admission: reservoir size R(t) is proportional to S(u) and to exp(k * H_t) (k is elasticity hyperparam).
5) Queueing model: reservoir is FIFO; if R fills, new requests are delayed to slowpath or throttled according to policy. We approximate p95 queue contribution via extreme-value tail model fit on simulated overflow counts.

Spreadsheet layout (tab-by-tab)

1) params - static knobs: token_ms_per_model, alpha_batching, baseline_slots, elasticity_k, window_ms, entropy_bins, short/med/long size thresholds, cost_per_slot_hour.
2) arrivals - synthetic generator: columns timestamp_ms, inter_arrival_ms, token_count, bucket, H_t (computed per line via rolling histogram). We include a few synthetic shapes: Poisson, clustered bursts (bursts of 10s at 50% higher rate), diurnal ramp, and a heavy-tailed arrival with occasional microbursts.
3) slot-supply - computes S(u) for rolling utilization: baseline_slots + elastic_slots = baseline + floor(elasticity_k * H_norm * baseline).
4) reservoir - sim engine that iterates timestamps applying admission rules, forms batches when a slot is assigned, computes realized batch_size, service_time, finish_time. Tracks queue lengths and overflow events.
5) metrics - computes per-minute p50/p95/p99, avg_tokens_per_slot, slot_utilization, cost_estimate = hours * cost_per_slot_hour, and unit_token_cost.
6) experiments - table of scenario rows: scenario_name, arrival_shape, elasticity_k, baseline_slots, R_target, p95, cost. We plan to run O(60) scenarios (grid over k in [0..2], baseline in [8,16,32], 4 arrival shapes).

Key equations (spreadsheet formulas described in plain terms)

- H_t = -sum_i p_i * log2(p_i) over inter-arrival histogram for last window. Normalize H_norm = H_t / H_max.
- elastic_slots = floor(baseline_slots * (exp(k * H_norm) - 1))
- effective_batch_time = token_ms_per_model * tokens_in_batch / E(batch_size)
- slot_finish_time = max(slot_available_at, request_arrival) + effective_batch_time

Quick sanity checks / calibration steps

- Calibrate alpha in E(batch_size) by running microbench for batch sizes 1..16 and fitting 1/(1+alpha*(n-1)). Put the raw bench numbers in params.
- Validate token_ms_per_model using profiler traces (PR: github.com/redwood-inference/serve/pull/1987).
- Confirm H_max by measuring entropy on 24h production traces (sampling). Constrain normalization accordingly.

Experiment plan (low friction)

1) Implement spreadsheet prototype (this doc -> sheet). Build synthetic arrival generator seeds so results are repeatable. (owner: Aisha)
2) Short-run bench: run microbench for batching alpha (owner: Lin).
3) Run 60 spreadsheet simulations overnight and gather scenario matrix (owner: Mateo).
4) Pick 3 candidate elasticity_k values and implement a small canary in staging that toggles reservoir size by exp(k*H_norm) with very conservative safety bounds (+/- 20%). Instrument p95 and overflow counters (owner: Priya).
5) Postmortem: if p95 improves with same or lower cost, promote to in_review and prepare a PR for default autoscaler heuristic.

Heuristics & recommended defaults (for prototype)

- baseline_slots = 16 for medium-sized model (tune per model family).
- elasticity_k initial guess = 0.8. This creates modest elasticity: at high entropy supply increases ~120%.
- reservoir_release_delay = 60ms (small grace period to coalesce microbursts).
- max_elastic_slots = baseline * 2 (safety cap).

Failure modes & risk mitigation

- Mis-estimated H_t: noisy entropy estimates can flip supply rapidly; mitigate with exponential smoothing on H_t (tau ~ 1s).
- Sim-to-real gap: synthetic arrivals miss cross-customer correlation; ensure canary stage has customer-mix sampling.
- Unexpected long-tail service times: introduce safety headroom and monitor slowpath rate.

Open questions

- What is the operational cost of computing H_t at 250ms frequency in the real control plane? (Lat/CPU cost tradeoff)
- How do we combine entropy from arrival times with token-length entropy (mixed request size unpredictability)?
- Do we need class-aware elasticity (separate pools for latency-critical endpoints)?

Next steps / todos

- [ ] Create spreadsheet with tabs described above and fill params with current perf numbers (Aisha, by 2025-11-11).
- [ ] Lin: run batch microbench and upload CSV to linked PR (due 2025-11-14).
- [ ] Mateo: run scenario grid and post result heatmap in #serving-runtime (due 2025-11-20).
- [ ] Priya: scope staging canary and alerting thresholds (due 2025-12-01).

Notes to reviewers

This is intentionally lightweight — focus on whether the arrival-entropy signal is a promising control knob compared to time-window heuristics used today. Main deliverable is a reproducible spreadsheet + a short sim-run that highlights p95 vs cost tradeoffs across 4 archetypal arrival shapes.
